## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{100}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can a better prediction still produce a worse physical action?_

A learned model can recognize a task correctly and still act too late to stop a moving machine or prevent excessive contact force. Once a command produces motion or heat, replacing the prediction cannot undo the work already delivered. The engineer must therefore connect model quality to the body's limits, the time available to respond, and the evidence supporting the next action. An independent permission path must be able to refuse a proposal and carry out a feasible fallback even when the model stalls. At the causal boundary, where commands become physical work, irreversibility makes these responsibilities part of the system's architecture.

- Derive the Kinematic Roofline to quantify how sense-to-act computational latency converts directly into irreversible physical stopping distance
- Classify machines by their dominant operating constraint: stopping clearance, contact force, or thermal and electrical margins
- Apply the three-criterion Physical AI scope test to separate advisory models and classical controllers from autonomous physical systems
- Locate the proposal boundary in the five-level machine model and explain why the permission path alone holds actuator-write authority
- Dissect the 2018 Tempe collision to diagnose how perception classification churn, action suppression delays, and disabled safety redundancy combine to cause catastrophic boundary failures
- Apply the four bedrock laws to connect physical limits, learned capability, runtime decisions, and evidence for operation
- Explain why physical authority is continuous and state-dependent, showing how safety, security, and accountability converge at the permission path

:::

## Artificial Intelligence Beyond Glass {#sec-boundary-beyond-glass}

A warehouse robot approaches the end of a storage rack while its learned model processes a camera image. A worker steps into the aisle before the model returns its next proposal. The computer can still discard that proposal, but the robot has continued moving throughout the calculation. Choosing an action therefore requires reasoning about both the prediction and the physical state in which it will execute.

For an advisory model, an output can be inspected or rejected before another system acts on it. Digital mistakes can still cause harm, and computation itself consumes energy. The distinction is that restoring a software state cannot restore the position of a moving robot or repair an object it has struck. The engineering problem begins with this difference and leads from physical limits to the architecture that checks each proposed action.

The physical plant is the apparatus being controlled, such as the robot's wheeled base or arm. Its physical state $\mathbf{x}(t)$ changes while the computer calculates. The dynamics $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, t)$ express how that state changes with the applied input and time. For the moving base, the immediate consequence follows from familiar kinematics. When a mobile robot of mass $m$ cruises at velocity $v = 1.5\text{ m/s}$ with acceleration $a$, it carries stored momentum $p = mv$ and kinetic energy $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. If the host processor stalls for an unguided pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}} = 100\text{ ms}$, the machine continues traveling before braking begins:
$$d = v \tau_{\text{delay}} + \frac{1}{2} a \tau_{\text{delay}}^2$$
At steady cruising speed ($a = 0$), this burns $d = v \tau_{\text{delay}} = 15\text{ cm}$ of clearance completely blind. If the machine is actively accelerating into a turn or ramping motor current ($a > 0$), the quadratic latency penalty $\frac{1}{2} a \tau_{\text{delay}}^2$ compounds the displacement, pushing the unguided plant even deeper into potential hazard before mechanical brakes can begin to bite. No software interrupt, exception handler, or thread abort can freeze that kinetic momentum in mid-air.

The warehouse example connects three engineering responsibilities. The model must recognize a useful action, the permission path must judge it while the observation is still relevant, and the body must be able to execute the admitted motion or a feasible fallback. A stronger prediction alone cannot recover clearance already consumed during computation. Designing physical AI therefore requires following the complete path from a learned proposal to motion and back to observation.

**Moravec's paradox**\index{Moravec's paradox}[^fn-ai-moravec-paradox] [@moravec1988mind] helps explain the interest in learning for physical tasks: sensorimotor skills that people perform with little conscious effort can be difficult to reproduce computationally. Learned models extend the range of scenes and tasks a machine can interpret. Their usefulness creates a further obligation to determine where demonstrated competence supports operation; @sec-evaluation-trial-limits develops the limits of that evidence.

[^fn-ai-moravec-paradox]: **Moravec's Paradox**\index{Moravec's Paradox}: The observation in artificial intelligence [@moravec1988mind] that high-level reasoning requires comparatively little computation, whereas low-level sensorimotor coordination demands enormous perceptual and computational resources.

When a machine acts, it changes the conditions of its next observation. This is the feedback perspective associated with cybernetics[^fn-boundary-wiener-feedback] [@wiener1948cybernetics]. The warehouse robot's movement changes both its distance from the worker and the next image available to its model.

[^fn-boundary-wiener-feedback]: **Cybernetic Feedback Loops**\index{Cybernetic Feedback Loops}: In Norbert Wiener's cybernetic framework [@wiener1948cybernetics], feedback denotes adjusting future action using past performance.

Building the complete loop requires contributions from several disciplines. Machine learning supplies perception and action proposals. Computer systems determine how quickly the computation and communication finish, including the limits imposed by memory traffic [@williams2009roofline]. Mechanics and control establish which motions the plant can sustain. Embedded systems enforce the timing and access rules that connect a proposal to an actuator. These responsibilities meet at a common decision: whether the proposed action can execute under the machine's current conditions. This book develops the reasoning needed to make and justify that decision.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The separation of learned proposals from actuation authority is mapped to isolated silicon domains in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning.
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {#dfn-boundary-physical-artificial-intelligence-physical-ai .callout-definition title="Physical artificial intelligence"}

***Physical artificial intelligence***\index{Physical Artificial Intelligence!definition}\index{Physical AI!definition} is the engineering of closed-loop machines in which learned models influence physical actions that change subsequent observations.

1.  **Significance**: Model performance becomes a property of an operating machine. Its actions must fit the plant's physical limits and the time available to respond.
2.  **Distinction**: The scope test later in this chapter combines a learned model, consequential physical feedback, and delegated physical authority. Neither a model used only for advice nor an automated machine without a learned component meets all three criteria.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the body as a peripheral device for a model. A useful proposal still needs an independent permission decision based on the current state, physical limits, and available fallback.

:::

The remainder of this chapter follows an action command from neural computation to mechanical work, compares the binding physical budgets of three machine classes, formalizes a three-criterion scope test to delineate the field, organizes the physical machine into five structural levels, and dissects the forensic record of the 2018 Tempe collision to diagnose how boundary violations occur. The concluding sections codify these insights into Four Bedrock Laws, establish where safety, security, and accountability converge, and outline the architectural spine of the book.

## Defining the Cyber-Physical Causal Boundary {#sec-boundary-causal-boundary}

An advisory model that displays an inference result on a screen or returns a JSON payload to a web client has no direct electrical or mechanical coupling to physical actuators. A human operator may inspect and discard the prediction, or downstream business logic may reject a candidate token before committing an external transaction.[^fn-math-idempotency-physical] Neither property makes digital errors benign: an operator may act on flawed recommendations, and an automated algorithmic trading engine may execute catastrophic financial transactions across electronic exchanges. The relevant distinction is whether the automated system can turn an accepted model proposal into physical action. Arbitration belongs inside that system; it protects the causal boundary rather than removing it.

[^fn-math-idempotency-physical]: **Idempotency**\index{Idempotency}: Repeating an idempotent operation has the same specified result as executing it once. A motor setpoint command can have idempotent command semantics, but repeated execution may still dissipate energy. Idempotency does not imply reversibility or harmlessness.

### Tensors to silicon and electromechanical transduction {#sec-boundary-tensors-to-silicon}

In modern computational frameworks, executing `action_chunk = policy(observation)` produces a floating-point tensor. The tensor describes a proposed action; moving the machine requires a chain of controllers and physical actuators. The causal boundary is the interface through which an admitted command changes the physical plant.

In modern robot learning architectures, the policy's output is typically an action chunk tensor of shape $[B, H, d_a]$, predicting a sequence of $H$ future waypoints (joint positions, angular velocities, or 6-DOF Cartesian poses) over an upcoming temporal horizon.[^fn-action-chunk-repr] In pure software, this tensor represents nothing more than a contiguous array of IEEE 754 floating-point values occupying GPU HBM or cache lines. It cannot execute directly on physical motors.

[^fn-action-chunk-repr]: **Action Chunk Representations**\index{Action Chunk Representations}: In robot learning literature [@zhao2023learning], action chunks are typically tensors of shape $[B, H, d_a]$ where $B$ is batch size, $H$ is the planning prediction horizon, and $d_a$ is action dimension (such as target joint positions $\hat{\mathbf{q}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ or 3D Cartesian position and orientation deltas). The formal spatial transformation representations are detailed in @sec-appendix-control-spatial; @sec-brain defines the chunk and its horizon.

The permission path checks whether the action chunk fits the current physical limits and can be carried out in time. If admitted, its setpoints pass to the controllers that drive the motors. A position controller determines the motion correction needed; the drive regulates electrical current to produce torque. @Sec-body develops the physical limits of this conversion, and @sec-nervous develops its timing and authority boundaries.

For a motor driven by pulse-width modulation (PWM), a software write sets a hardware timer's switching command. The power electronics use that signal to control current in the motor windings. Electromagnetic torque then accelerates the rotor and attached mechanism. This example establishes the distinction needed here: changing a proposed setpoint in memory is different from changing a command that has already produced motion. A later command can brake or redirect the machine, but that response takes time and must itself remain physically feasible.

::: {#dfn-boundary-causal-boundary .callout-definition title="Causal boundary"}

***Causal boundary***\index{Causal boundary!definition} is the interface through which a digital command produces physical forces, currents, or flows.

1.  **Significance**: A proposal can be rejected before it changes the plant. Once executed, it can alter the environment, dissipate energy, and change subsequent observations.
2.  **Distinction**: Restoring a command in memory does not restore the machine's prior physical state. Recovery requires another physical action, with its own limits and consequences.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Assuming that canceling a software task stops the motion it initiated. The machine needs a feasible stopping or holding response even when its proposer stops computing.

:::

An offline test can hold its examples fixed regardless of the model's predictions. A robot cannot generally rely on that separation: turning the chassis changes the next camera view, and pushing an object changes its location. The learning problem must account for observations that depend on earlier actions.

In a physical system, the environment evolves in a closed causal loop: the next physical state $\mathbf{s}_{t+1}$ and incoming sensor observation $\mathbf{o}_{t+1}$ depend directly on the action $\mathbf{a}_t$ produced by the prior model inference. The sensory input stream is endogenous, governed by continuous closed-loop dynamics:
$$\mathbf{s}_{t+1} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t), \quad \mathbf{o}_{t+1} \sim p(\mathbf{o} \mid \mathbf{s}_{t+1})$$

An erroneous action can therefore move the machine into states poorly represented in its training data. Errors in those states may produce further departures from the demonstrated behavior (@fig-01-causal-loop). This possibility motivates closed-loop evaluation; it does not mean that every error necessarily produces an unstable trajectory.

::: {#fig-01-causal-loop fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The closed causal loop**: Advisory output (top) stops at an informational interface. In physical AI (bottom), permitted model proposals reach hardware registers, where electrical current produces force and motion. Those actions alter the environment and subsequent sensor observations." fig-alt="Flowchart contrasting advisory predictions with physical AI. The upper path ends at an informational interface; the lower path carries sensor observations to a proposal, the permission path, motor actuators, and a changing physical plant."}
![](images/svg/fig01_causal_loop.svg){width="95%"}
:::

Because physical mass possesses inertia and computation takes finite real time, latency in physical AI translates directly into physical displacement. As shown on the autonomous testbed in @fig-01-sensor-rack, real-world robotic systems rely on dense multi-modal sensor suites (spinning lidar scanners, camera arrays, and radar units) that continuously stream high-bandwidth telemetry to onboard processors. Every stage in this pipeline—from photodiode photon integration and sensor bus serialization,[^fn-hw-serdes-bus] to neural inference on accelerator silicon and packet transmission over deterministic fieldbuses—consumes real-world milliseconds.

[^fn-hw-serdes-bus]: **Automotive Serializer/Deserializer (SerDes)**\index{SerDes!sensor links}: High-speed physical-layer links (such as FPD-Link or GMSL) that transport uncompressed, low-latency multi-gigabit video streams over lightweight coaxial or shielded twisted-pair cables. Combined with dedicated hardware trigger lines, SerDes interfaces ensure microsecond-synchronized shutter capture across the sensor ring. For bus specifications, see @sec-appendix-systems.

::: {#fig-01-sensor-rack fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Lidar sensor ingress**: A 64-beam spinning optical lidar assembly mounted aboard an autonomous research testbed. In physical AI, sensor streams delivering over 1.3 million points per second must be serialized over real-time hardware interfaces, synchronized to microsecond timestamps, and processed through neural perception backbones within strict latency deadlines. (Source: Steve Jurvetson, CC BY 2.0)." fig-alt="Close-up photograph of a roof-mounted 64-beam spinning optical lidar sensor assembly on an autonomous research vehicle testbed, showing optical lenses and aluminum housing."}

### Kinematic rooflines and latency-to-clearance translation {#sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline}

```{python}
#| label: boundary-blind-travel
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BLIND TRAVEL OF THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The blind-travel paragraph in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary.
# │ Goal: Convert the running machine's total pre-brake delay into distance.
# │ Show: Drive limit, total pre-brake delay, and travel before braking begins.
# │ How: v * tau_delay from the warehouse mobile manipulator and its aisle
# │      scenario in mlsysim; no value is retyped here.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class BlindTravel:
    """Travel of the running machine's base before braking begins (illustrative inputs)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (capture to retarding force)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    blind = (v * tau_delay).to(millimeter)
    blind_display = round(blind.to(millimeter).magnitude) * millimeter

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Canon drive limit is 1.5 m/s, got {v}.")
    check(abs(tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude - 133.6) < 5e-3, f"Canon tau_delay is 133.6 ms, got {tau_delay}.")
    check(abs(blind.to(millimeter).magnitude - 200.4) < 5e-3, f"Canon blind travel is 200 mm, got {blind}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    blind_str = fmt_length(blind_display, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

As a concrete example, consider the wheeled base of a warehouse mobile manipulator (introduced in full in @sec-boundary-three-classes), cruising down an aisle at its `{python} BlindTravel.v_str` drive limit (illustrative; see the Reader Guide). Its pre-brake delay, which later chapters assemble term by term, is at most `{python} BlindTravel.tau_delay_str`, spanning the interval from the initial optical capture of a person stepping out from behind a storage rack to the physical onset of caliper friction force. Over that unguided interval, the base travels `{python} BlindTravel.blind_str` with zero mechanical response to the incoming visual evidence. If an obstacle or human worker emerges within that blind distance, collision occurs before the actuators can apply a single Newton of retarding force—and no amount of neural network capacity, training data, or model scale can alter that physical reality.

This fundamental trade-off between computational delay and physical clearance is formalized by the **kinematic roofline**\index{Kinematic roofline}, the physical counterpart to the computer architecture Roofline Model [@williams2009roofline]. In microprocessor and accelerator design, Patterson and Williams bound attainable computational throughput ($\text{FLOP/s}$) by the lower of two hard hardware ceilings:
$$\text{Attainable Performance} \le \min\Big(\text{Peak Arithmetic Throughput}, \; \text{Operational Intensity} \times \text{Peak Memory Bandwidth}\Big)$$
where operational intensity (measured in $\text{FLOPs/byte}$) determines whether an execution kernel is compute-bound by floating-point ALUs or memory-bound by interconnect throughput.

In Physical AI systems, the physical dual of the Patterson compute roofline bounds achievable operational velocity by the lower of multiple interacting physical ceilings:
$$v_{\max} \le \min\big(v_{\text{budget}}, \; v_{\text{track}}, \; v_{\text{thermal}}\big)$$
where $v_{\text{track}}$ is the dynamic trajectory tracking ceiling enforced by closed-loop actuator bandwidth, $v_{\text{thermal}}$ is the continuous velocity limit imposed by winding Joule heating and power dissipation, and $v_{\text{budget}}$ is the kinematic stopping velocity bound enforced by the perception horizon $R_{\text{sensor}}$, sense-to-act latency $\tau_{\text{delay}}$, and mechanical braking deceleration $a_{\text{brake}}$.

While the Patterson compute roofline selects the minimum of arithmetic and memory bandwidth bounds because execution pipelines and memory controllers operate concurrently to hide latency, the physical stopping budget $v_{\text{budget}}$ arises because physical stopping clearance *adds* two distinct physical penalties that execute strictly sequentially in real time:
$$d_{\text{stop}}(v, \tau_{\text{delay}}, a) = \underbrace{v \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}} + \frac{1}{2} a \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}}^2}_{\text{computational blind travel}} + \underbrace{\frac{v_{\text{brake}}^2}{2 a_{\text{brake}}}}_{\text{mechanical energy dissipation}} \le R_{\text{sensor}}$$
where $a$ is the forward acceleration prior to braking and $v_{\text{brake}} = v + a \tau_{\text{delay}}$ is the physical velocity at the exact instant mechanical retarding force begins. At steady cruising velocity ($a = 0$), $v_{\text{brake}} = v$, and the relation simplifies to $d_{\text{stop}} = v \tau_{\text{delay}} + \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{brake}}}$. When the machine is actively accelerating ($a > 0$), however, the quadratic term $\frac{1}{2} a \tau_{\text{delay}}^2$ severely compounds blind displacement, and higher kinetic energy must be shed by mechanical brakes.

Under emergency braking, total stopping clearance $d_{\text{stop}}$ is the sum of computational blind travel (which scales with end-to-end delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$, initial velocity $v$, and acceleration $a$) and mechanical braking distance (which scales quadratically with braking velocity $v_{\text{brake}}^2$ under the work-energy theorem). @Sec-body-kinetic-momentum formally derives this relationship from Newtonian mechanics. Machine learning systems engineers frequently fall prey to "kernel myopia"—measuring only GPU forward-pass inference latency ($\tau_{\text{compute}} \approx 15\text{--}20\text{ ms}$) and assuming the robot operates with a $20\text{ ms}$ reaction time. In physical AI, the true sense-to-act delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ spans a strictly sequential causal pipeline: photodiode photon integration and rolling shutter readout ($\tau_{\text{sensor}} \approx 10\text{--}33\text{ ms}$), SerDes serialization and PCIe DMA ring-buffer transfers ($\tau_{\text{transport}} \approx 5\text{--}10\text{ ms}$), neural tensor-core execution ($\tau_{\text{compute}}$), lockstep safety arbitration across barrier certificates ($\tau_{\text{arbitration}} \approx 1\text{--}2\text{ ms}$), cyclic fieldbus transmission over EtherCAT or CAN-FD ($\tau_{\text{fieldbus}} \approx 1\text{--}2\text{ ms}$), and actuator FOC current rise and brake caliper pressure buildup ($\tau_{\text{actuator}} \approx 20\text{--}50\text{ ms}$). The blind travel is non-negotiable: during this entire window, no retarding torque can yet exist at the wheels. As @tbl-01-kinematic-roofline demonstrates across representative embodied platforms, the delay's fractional share of the total stopping envelope is largest for agile, low-speed systems, while its absolute displacement reaches multi-meter vehicle lengths at highway speeds.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-kinematic-roofline
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ KINEMATIC ROOFLINE NOMOGRAM (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-01-kinematic-roofline (cells and caption) and the paragraph
# │          after it (the heavier-model example).
# │ Goal: Show how a fixed delay before braking adds to braking distance for
# │       platforms of increasing speed.
# │ Show: Braking distance, stopping distance at three delays, and the delay
# │       share of the stop at the longest delay, per platform.
# │ How: d_stop = v*tau + v^2/(2a) via calc_safe_stopping_distance. The running
# │      machine's row reads its drive limit and credible deceleration from
# │      mlsysim; the other three rows are generic platform classes whose
# │      speeds and decelerations are scenario assumptions for the contrast.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_percent, check
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle
_MPS = meter / second
_MPS2 = meter / second**2

def _roofline_row(v, a, taus):
    """Braking distance, stopping distances, delay travel, and delay share at the last delay."""
    brake = (v**2 / (2 * a)).to(meter)
    totals = [calc_safe_stopping_distance(v, t, a) for t in taus]
    adds = [(v * t).to(ureg.centimeter) for t in taus]
    share = (adds[-1] / totals[-1]).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    return brake, totals, adds, share

def _sig3_length(d):
    """A distance in meters to three significant figures (half up), with its decimal count."""
    x = Decimal(repr(d.to(meter).magnitude))
    places = max(0, 2 - x.adjusted())
    return float(x.quantize(Decimal(1).scaleb(-places), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)) * meter, places

def _fmt_sig3(d):
    """Format a distance in meters to three significant figures."""
    rounded, places = _sig3_length(d)
    if float(rounded.magnitude).is_integer():
        places = 0  # the formatter forbids trailing zeros on integer-like values
    return fmt_length(rounded, unit=meter, precision=places)

def _roofline_strs(v, a, taus):
    """Formatted table cells for one platform row: one precision rule per column."""
    brake, totals, adds, share = _roofline_row(v, a, taus)
    cells = [f"{_fmt_sig3(t)} (+{fmt_length(d, unit=ureg.centimeter)})" for t, d in zip(totals, adds)]
    return (
        fmt_velocity(v, unit=_MPS),
        fmt_velocity(v, unit=kilometer / hour),
        fmt_acceleration(a, unit=_MPS2),
        fmt((a / ureg.standard_gravity).to("dimensionless").magnitude, precision=2, suffix=" g"),
        _fmt_sig3(brake),
        cells[0],
        cells[1],
        cells[2],
        fmt_percent(share, precision=1, style="symbol"),
    )

class KinematicRoofline:
    """Stopping distance against delay for four platform classes (illustrative inputs)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    tau_reflex = 10 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (reflex-class delay column)
    tau_fast = 50 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (short-class delay column)
    tau_vla = 200 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (long-class delay column)
    hum_v = 1.0 * _MPS  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption, humanoid or quadruped)
    hum_a = 4.0 * _MPS2  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption)
    rm_v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (running machine drive limit)
    rm_a = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (running machine credible deceleration)
    bot_v = 6.0 * _MPS  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption, urban delivery robot)
    bot_a = 4.5 * _MPS2  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption)
    av_v = 20.0 * _MPS  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption, passenger vehicle)
    av_a = 7.0 * _MPS2  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption)
    model_extra = 150 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption, heavier model)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    taus = [tau_reflex, tau_fast, tau_vla]
    hum_brake, hum_totals, hum_adds, hum_share = _roofline_row(hum_v, hum_a, taus)
    rm_brake, rm_totals, rm_adds, rm_share = _roofline_row(rm_v, rm_a, taus)
    bot_brake, bot_totals, bot_adds, bot_share = _roofline_row(bot_v, bot_a, taus)
    av_brake, av_totals, av_adds, av_share = _roofline_row(av_v, av_a, taus)
    av_vla_travel = (av_v * tau_vla).to(meter)
    av_extra_travel = (av_v * model_extra).to(meter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(
        abs(rm_v.to(_MPS).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9 and abs(rm_a.to(_MPS2).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9,
        "The running machine row is canon: 1.5 m/s at 2.0 m/s^2.",
    )
    check(abs(rm_brake.to(meter).magnitude - 0.5625) < 1e-9, f"Canon braking at 1.5 m/s is 562.5 mm, got {rm_brake}.")
    check(abs(rm_totals[-1].to(meter).magnitude - 0.8625) < 1e-9, f"Running machine stop at 200 ms is 0.8625 m, got {rm_totals[-1]}.")
    check(abs(rm_share - 0.3478) < 5e-4, f"Delay share of the running machine's stop is about 34.8 percent, got {rm_share}.")
    check(hum_share > rm_share > bot_share > av_share, "The delay share must fall as platform speed rises.")
    check(abs(bot_brake.to(meter).magnitude - 4.0) < 1e-9, f"Delivery robot braking is 4.00 m, got {bot_brake}.")
    check(abs(av_vla_travel.to(meter).magnitude - 4.0) < 1e-9, "The caption claims 4 m of travel for the vehicle at 200 ms.")
    check(abs(av_extra_travel.to(meter).magnitude - 3.0) < 1e-9, "The prose claims 3 m of travel for 150 ms at highway speed.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_reflex_str = fmt_latency(tau_reflex, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_fast_str = fmt_latency(tau_fast, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_vla_str = fmt_latency(tau_vla, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    hum_v_str, hum_kmh_str, hum_a_str, hum_g_str, hum_brake_str, hum_t1_str, hum_t2_str, hum_t3_str, hum_share_str = _roofline_strs(
        hum_v, hum_a, taus
    )
    rm_v_str, rm_kmh_str, rm_a_str, rm_g_str, rm_brake_str, rm_t1_str, rm_t2_str, rm_t3_str, rm_share_str = _roofline_strs(rm_v, rm_a, taus)
    bot_v_str, bot_kmh_str, bot_a_str, bot_g_str, bot_brake_str, bot_t1_str, bot_t2_str, bot_t3_str, bot_share_str = _roofline_strs(
        bot_v, bot_a, taus
    )
    av_v_str, av_kmh_str, av_a_str, av_g_str, av_brake_str, av_t1_str, av_t2_str, av_t3_str, av_share_str = _roofline_strs(av_v, av_a, taus)
    av_vla_travel_str = fmt_length(av_vla_travel, unit=meter, precision=0)
    model_extra_str = fmt_latency(model_extra, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    av_extra_travel_str = fmt_length(av_extra_travel, unit=meter, precision=0)
```

: **Kinematic roofline nomogram**: Stopping clearance trade-offs across embodied platforms. The warehouse mobile manipulator's row uses its drive limit and credible deceleration. The three delay columns are classes of pre-brake delay, not the delay of any one platform. Stopping distances are rounded to three significant figures, and the added blind travel is given in centimeters to the nearest millimeter. At `{python} KinematicRoofline.tau_vla_str` of delay, an autonomous passenger car travels an additional `{python} KinematicRoofline.av_vla_travel_str`, an entire vehicle length, before its brakes engage. {#tbl-01-kinematic-roofline}

Just as an architect cannot resolve a memory-bound arithmetic pipeline by adding more ALU execution units, an autonomous vehicle systems engineer cannot resolve an emergency stopping clearance violation by adding model parameters if doing so lengthens the delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ before braking. A heavier foundation model that adds `{python} KinematicRoofline.model_extra_str` of computation consumes an extra `{python} KinematicRoofline.av_extra_travel_str` of physical travel at highway speeds, distance that no friction brake or collision-avoidance logic can recover.

The physical reality of this trade-off is captured longitudinally across five decades of autonomous vehicle systems (@fig-boundary-latency-vs-velocity). Why does physical stopping clearance impose such an unyielding limit? Before mechanical brakes can apply retarding force, the machine coasts at cruising velocity $v$ over the unguided reaction window $\tau_{\text{delay}}$, consuming a blind translation distance $d_{\text{blind}} = v \tau_{\text{delay}}$. Once the brakes engage, the work-energy theorem governs physical stopping: friction force $F_{\text{brake}} = m a_{\max}$ must dissipate the stored kinetic energy $E_k = \frac{1}{2}m v^2$ over the active braking distance $d_{\text{brake}} = \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\max}}$. The vehicle comes to rest only after traveling the sum of both distances, which must strictly fit within the reliable perception horizon $R_{\text{sensor}}$. The safe operating speed of any physical AI platform is therefore strictly bounded by the **kinematic stopping roofline**:
$$d_{\text{stop}} = \underbrace{v \tau_{\text{delay}}}_{\text{computational blind travel}} + \underbrace{\frac{v^2}{2 a_{\max}}}_{\text{mechanical dissipation}} \le R_{\text{sensor}}$$
where $v$ is vehicle velocity, $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ is the end-to-end sense-to-act loop latency, $a_{\max}$ is emergency braking deceleration ($0.7\,\text{g} \approx 6.86\,\text{m/s}^2$ on dry asphalt), and $R_{\text{sensor}}$ is the effective sensor perception horizon.

Solving this quadratic inequality for velocity $v$ yields the exact stopping velocity ceiling:
$$v \le v_{\text{budget}}(\tau_{\text{delay}}) = \sqrt{(a_{\max} \tau_{\text{delay}})^2 + 2 a_{\max} R_{\text{sensor}}} - a_{\max} \tau_{\text{delay}}$$
Along with the dynamic actuator tracking limit ($v_{\text{track}}$) and the continuous thermal dissipation limit ($v_{\text{thermal}}$), the attainable operating envelope of the physical agent is governed by the multi-budget kinematic roofline $v_{\max} \le \min(v_{\text{budget}}, v_{\text{track}}, v_{\text{thermal}})$.

This formulation reveals why learned artificial intelligence cannot simply scale out of stopping distances:

1. **Mechanical friction is invariant to model scale:** The deceleration term $\frac{v^2}{2 a_{\max}}$ is dictated by classical tire-road friction ($\mu$) and gravity ($a_{\max} \approx \mu g$). No increase in neural network parameter count, self-attention depth, or pretraining dataset size can alter the physical friction coefficient between rubber and asphalt or the shear stress of a mechanical brake rotor.
2. **Computational scaling worsens blind travel:** In conventional software, empirical scaling laws show that larger models achieve lower loss. In physical systems, however, scaling model capacity expands the computational graph, increasing memory bus traffic, KV-cache pressure, and inference execution time. If scaling a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy adds just `{python} KinematicRoofline.model_extra_str` of tail latency to $\tau_{\text{delay}}$, an autonomous vehicle cruising at highway speeds ($20\text{ m/s}$) travels an extra `{python} KinematicRoofline.av_extra_travel_str` completely blind before physical braking begins. At $30\text{ m/s}$ ($108\text{ km/h}$), that delay burns $4.5\text{ m}$ of critical clearance.
3. **The safety trade-off inverts:** A larger model with superior semantic classification can easily yield a *less safe* physical machine if its added computational delay expands the stopping distance faster than its perceptual acuity can compensate. You cannot scale parameters to outrun kinetic energy.

Understanding the geometry of @fig-boundary-latency-vs-velocity requires analyzing the kinematic stopping equation across two distinct asymptotic regimes on the log-log axes:

1. **The mechanical braking ceiling ($\tau_{\text{delay}} \to 0$):** When computation is instantaneous relative to the vehicle's deceleration timescale, the stopping distance is dominated entirely by mechanical friction braking: $d_{\text{stop}} \approx v^2 / (2 a_{\max}) \le R_{\text{sensor}}$, yielding the velocity asymptote $v \le \sqrt{2 a_{\max} R_{\text{sensor}}}$. On log-log coordinates, this appears as the flat horizontal plateau on the left side of each curve. In this regime, reducing algorithmic latency yields diminishing returns; maximum safe speed is constrained strictly by tire-road friction or actuator brake torque ($a_{\max} \approx 0.7\,\text{g} = 6.86\,\text{m/s}^2$) and perceptual range ($R_{\text{sensor}}$).
2. **The computational latency cliff ($\tau_{\text{delay}} \gg \sqrt{2 R_{\text{sensor}} / a_{\max}}$):** When latency dominates, the distance traveled blind during computational deliberation vastly exceeds the distance traveled during active braking: $d_{\text{stop}} \approx v \tau_{\text{delay}} \le R_{\text{sensor}}$, yielding the linear velocity ceiling $v \le R_{\text{sensor}} / \tau_{\text{delay}}$. Taking logarithms produces $\log v \le \log R_{\text{sensor}} - \log \tau_{\text{delay}}$, which forms the steep $-45^\circ$ diagonal asymptote (slope of $-1$) on the right. In this computational regime, every tenfold increase in latency forces a tenfold reduction in operational velocity to avoid out-driving the perception horizon.

Any operating point residing above the $R_{\text{sensor}} = 200\,\text{m}$ envelope enters the shaded red **physically unrecoverable regime**. Within this domain, stopping distance exceeds the maximum perceptual range of even long-range automotive lidar and radar, rendering collision avoidance mathematically impossible regardless of downstream trajectory planning or model capacity.

The historical trajectory across five decades maps this fundamental frontier. In the early deliberative era (1970–1980), SRI's Shakey and Moravec's Stanford Cart operated with loop latencies between $15$ and $30\,\text{seconds}$ due to offboard mainframe compute bottlenecks, capping safe crawl speeds below $0.2\,\text{km/h}$. By the mid-1980s and 1990s, Ernst Dickmanns' VaMoRs demonstrated that running custom 4D dynamic vision algorithms at $25\,\text{Hz}$ ($\tau = 40\,\text{ms}$) unlocked $96\,\text{km/h}$ highway speeds on the German Autobahn, proving that control loop cadence—rather than raw cognitive deliberation depth—governs safe mobility. During the DARPA Grand Challenges (2004–2007), Stanford Stanley and CMU Boss operated at $10\text{--}12\,\text{Hz}$ ($85\text{--}100\,\text{ms}$) to navigate desert trails and urban intersections at $48\text{--}60\,\text{km/h}$. Today, production robotaxis such as the Waymo Driver maintain $\sim 80\,\text{ms}$ loop latencies to ensure stopping envelopes remain well within their $200\,\text{m}$ sensor horizons at highway velocities ($110\,\text{km/h}$), while autonomous racing vehicles (such as the Indy Autonomous Challenge PoliMOVE team) push loop latencies down to $28\,\text{ms}$ ($>35\,\text{Hz}$) to operate safely at speeds exceeding $309\,\text{km/h}$.

::: {#fig-boundary-latency-vs-velocity fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The causal boundary: sense-to-act loop latency vs. vehicle operational speed envelope (1970–2026)**: Empirical milestones spanning five decades of autonomous ground vehicles plotted against physical kinematic stopping rooflines under emergency deceleration ($a_{\\max} = 0.7\\,\\text{g} = 6.86\\,\\text{m/s}^2$) across four sensor horizons ($R = 5\\,\\text{m}$ to $200\\,\\text{m}$). Vehicles above the $R = 200\\,\\text{m}$ ceiling enter the physically unrecoverable regime, where stopping distance exceeds sensor range regardless of downstream algorithm cleverness. Milestones: SRI Shakey (1970), Stanford Cart (1979), CMU Navlab 1 (1986), UniBwM VaMoRs (1987), CMU Navlab 5 (1995), Stanford Stanley (2005), CMU Boss (2007), Waymo Driver Gen 5/6 (2024), and Indy Autonomous Challenge PoliMOVE AV-24 (2024)." fig-alt="Log-log scatter plot of sense-to-act loop latency from 10 milliseconds to 60 seconds against operational vehicle speed from 0.1 to 350 km/h. Four kinematic roofline curves show maximum safe speeds for sensor horizons from 5 to 200 meters. Historical vehicles are plotted from Shakey at 30 seconds and 0.18 km/h to modern Indy Autonomous racing at 28 milliseconds and 309 km/h, highlighting shaded eras from Deliberative (1970-1980) to High-Speed Real-Time (2020-2026)."}

### Thermodynamic irreversibility and the closed loop {#sec-boundary-thermodynamic-irreversibility}

A checkpoint can restore the logical state of a computation. It cannot reverse the energy consumed by that computation, and it cannot undo an external action taken from its output. The distinction needed for physical AI is therefore between restoring a software state and restoring the physical world. A motor command that has already moved a load belongs to the latter problem.

In physical machines, computational abstraction collides with macroscopic thermodynamics. At the microscopic limit, Landauer's principle establishes a theoretical minimum computational dissipation of $k_B T \ln 2 \approx 2.87 \times 10^{-21}\text{ J}$ at $300\text{ K}$ per erased bit.[^fn-phys-landauer-limit] In physical AI systems, however, the dominant irreversibility is macroscopic—operating twenty-four orders of magnitude above the Landauer threshold. Motor inverters draw tens to hundreds of Amperes from high-voltage DC battery rails, dissipating kilowatt-scale resistive Joule heating ($I_{\text{phase}}^2 R_{\text{winding}}$) in the stator windings and imparting hundreds or thousands of Joules of kinetic energy to mechanical linkages.

If an erroneous model proposal commands excessive torque and drives an articulated manipulator into a rigid workcell fixture, that kinetic energy converts instantaneously into plastic deformation of the end-effector, yield strain across harmonic drive gear teeth, and acoustic and thermal dissipation. Under the Second Law of Thermodynamics, macroscopic entropy generation is strictly irreversible. No operating system exception handler, signal trap, or checkpoint restore can extract that mechanical work from the deformed metal, reverse physical material failure, or pull dissipated heat back from the environment.

[^fn-phys-landauer-limit]: **Thermodynamic Limits of Computation**\index{Thermodynamic Limits of Computation}: At a fundamental level, @landauer1961 established that erasing logical bits dissipates at least $k_B T \ln 2$ of heat per erased bit. In physical AI systems, however, the dominant irreversibility is macroscopic: motor inverters draw tens of Amperes from battery packs, dissipating kilowatt-scale Joule heat ($I^2 R$) and imparting momentum to moving linkages.

Because physical actuation cannot be rolled back, safety cannot be implemented as an asynchronous monitor, a post-hoc error recovery handler, or an unverified training penalty. The verification and admission of an action must occur *strictly ahead of time*, within a hard deterministic deadline bounded by the physical plant's rate of kinetic or thermal accumulation. The causal boundary marks the conversion of a command into physical work. Restoring the command's earlier value does not restore the earlier physical state.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The non-smooth contact mechanics and torque saturation limits governing motor irreversibility are derived in @sec-body-actuator-limits.
:::

class MachineLevelRates:
